items.title: Lesson 3, Focus Question: What happens to a laser beam when it passes from air into a swimming pool?

answer.html: Part of the light is reflected at the surface and part is transmitted into the water. The transmitted light slows down (water has 𝑛= 1.33, so 𝑣= 𝑐/ 𝑛 is smaller than in air) while its frequency stays the same, so its wavelength shortens. If the beam strikes the surface at an angle, its direction changes (refraction) according to Snell's law, 𝑛<sub>1</sub>sin𝜃<sub>1</sub> = 𝑛<sub>2</sub>sin𝜃<sub>2</sub>, and because water has a higher 𝑛 than air the beam bends toward the normal.

items.title: Lesson 3, Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question: Use what you learned in this lesson to explain again how a video can cross an ocean through an undersea cable.

answer.html: The video is carried as pulses of light in glass fibers. Light stays inside because the core's index of refraction is greater than the cladding's, so light striking the boundary at more than the critical angle, 𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>= sin<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>(𝑛<sub>2</sub> / 𝑛<sub>1</sub>), undergoes total internal reflection. Refraction determines how light enters and leaves the fiber, and dispersion (the dependence of 𝑛 on wavelength) is why pulses containing different wavelengths can spread out over long distances.

answer.html: 𝑛= 1.43. The index of refraction and the speed are inversely related (𝑛= 𝑐/ 𝑣): the higher the 𝑛, the slower light travels in the medium (and the shorter its wavelength, 𝜆= 𝜆<sub>0</sub> / 𝑛).

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It?: Compare transmitting data through a fiber-optic cable with sending it by a microwave tower relay.

answer.html: Similar: both carry digital information encoded in electromagnetic waves (light in fibers, microwaves between towers). Different: fiber guides the light inside glass by total internal reflection, so there is little loss, very high bandwidth, no weather interference, and good security, but a cable must be laid along the whole route. A microwave relay needs only a line of sight between towers, so it can be set up across rivers or rough terrain without digging, but its bandwidth is lower, rain and fog weaken the signal, and the beam spreads out so it can be intercepted.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 22 prompt (Apply): Over cold ocean water, the air just above the surface is cooler than the air higher up. Where do light waves travel faster, near the water or higher in the air?

body.html: Cooler air is denser and has a slightly larger index of refraction, so light travels more slowly in it (𝑣= 𝑐/ 𝑛).

answer.html: Higher up. The air near the cold water is cooler and has the larger 𝑛, so light travels more slowly there; the warmer air higher up has the smaller 𝑛 and light is faster. This is the reverse of a desert mirage, and it bends light waves downward, which can make distant ships appear lifted above the horizon.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 24 prompt: You and a friend standing 100 m apart both look at the same rainbow. Are you looking at the same rainbow? Can either of you walk to the end of it?

answer.html: No. A rainbow is not an object at a fixed place; it is sunlight reflected and refracted by many raindrops that sends light to your eye at a particular angle (about 42° from the line pointing away from the Sun). You and your friend receive light from different drops, so each sees a different rainbow, and if either of you moves, the rainbow moves too, so there is no end to reach.

items.title: Lesson 3, Check Your Progress 42: On a rainy morning the Sun is low in the east, 20° above the horizon. Which way should you look to see a rainbow, and how high above the horizon is the top of the primary bow (which is 42° from the point opposite the Sun)?

body.html: A rainbow is seen with the Sun behind you, centered on the point directly opposite the Sun.
The Sun is in the east, so the opposite point is toward the west, at 20° below the horizon. The top of the bow is 42° above that point, so its height above the horizon is 42° −20° = 22°.

items.title: Lesson 3, Focus Question: What happens to light when it enters a new medium?

answer.html: Part of the light is reflected and part is transmitted. The transmitted light changes speed (it slows in a medium with a higher index of refraction) while its frequency stays the same, so its wavelength changes too. If it strikes the boundary at an angle, its direction changes (refraction) according to Snell's law, 𝑛<sub>1</sub>sin𝜃<sub>1</sub> = 𝑛<sub>2</sub>sin𝜃<sub>2</sub>: toward the normal when entering a higher-𝑛 medium and away from the normal when entering a lower-𝑛 medium.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 18 prompt: What is the relationship between the angle of the light at the boundary and refraction?

For a given pair of media, a larger angle of incidence gives a larger angle of refraction (but not in direct proportion, because of the sine). At 𝜃<sub>1</sub> = 0° there is no bending at all. For the same 𝜃<sub>1</sub>, the larger 𝑛<sub>2</sub> is (water 1.33, glass 1.52, diamond 2.42), the more the ray bends toward the normal.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It?: Relationship between index of refraction and speed of light in a medium

answer.html: They are inversely related: 𝑛= 𝑐/ 𝑣. The higher the index of refraction, the slower the light travels in the medium (and the smaller the wavelength, 𝜆= 𝜆<sub>0</sub> / 𝑛).

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It?: Compare fiber-optic transmission with satellite transmission

answer.html: Similar: both carry digital information encoded in electromagnetic waves (light in fibers; microwaves/radio via satellite) at the speed of light in the medium. Different: fiber guides light inside glass by total internal reflection, so there is little loss, high bandwidth, no interference from weather, and good security, but cables must be laid along the whole route. A satellite link broadcasts through space and atmosphere, can reach remote or moving receivers without cables, but has lower bandwidth, signals are weakened and spread out, are affected by weather, and have a longer delay (a geostationary satellite is about 36 000 km up, so a round trip adds roughly a quarter second).

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 22 prompt (Apply): Where do light waves travel faster, near the road or near the top of the vehicle?

answer.html: Near the road. The air there is hotter, which gives it a smaller index of refraction, so light travels faster (𝑣= 𝑐/ 𝑛) than in the cooler air higher up. This is what bends the wavefronts upward.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 24 prompt: Can a rainbow be close enough to touch?

answer.html: No. A rainbow is not an object at a fixed place; it is light from many different droplets that reaches your eye at specific angles (about 42° from the line pointing away from the Sun). Each observer sees light from different droplets, and when you move, the rainbow moves with you, so you can never reach it.

answer.html: 1.33 < 𝑛<sub>liquid</sub> < 1.52

items.title: Lesson 3, Check Your Progress 40: Quartz or float glass for fiber cladding?

body.html: Total internal reflection needs the core to have the higher index; the cladding must have the lower 𝑛.

Float glass (𝑛= 1.52) has a lower index than quartz (𝑛= 1.54). With a quartz core and float-glass cladding, 𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>= sin<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>(1.52 / 1.54) = 80.8° (rays hitting the boundary at more than 80.8° from the normal are trapped).

answer.html: Use float glass for the cladding (lower 𝑛), with the higher-index material (quartz) as the core, so that light striking the boundary is totally internally reflected.

answer.html: For ordinary transparent media, no. 𝑛< 1 would mean 𝑣> 𝑐, that is, light moving faster than its speed in a vacuum, which would violate relativity. (Vacuum is 𝑛= 1.00, the lowest.)
